text:
Can you help me write the project summary for a grant application? I'm the managing attorney at a two-lawyer legal aid clinic that represents tenants facing eviction. We're applying to our state bar foundation for $90,000 to hire a third attorney for two years.

Facts:
- Last year 1,140 eviction cases were filed in our county. We represented the tenant in 163 of them.
- In the cases where we represented the tenant, 58% ended with the tenant staying in the home or getting at least 60 days to move. We don't have a comparable number for tenants without a lawyer.
- We turned away about 300 tenants last year because no attorney was free.
- Our two attorneys each carry about 80 open cases. One of them is leaving in June.
- A third attorney would cost $78,000 a year with benefits. The foundation's maximum award is $45,000 a year.
- The county gives us $60,000 a year, and that contract is up for renewal in October.

The project summary has to be 300 words or less.

Before I draft, a few questions. Each answer changes what the summary says or how it handles a weak point a reviewer will notice.

1. **How will you cover the gap between the grant and the cost?** The attorney costs $78,000 a year and the foundation pays at most $45,000, which leaves $33,000 a year. Where does that come from? Related: what's the status of the $60,000 county contract? Was it renewed this October, is it pending, or is the renewal next October? Reviewers will check whether the position can actually be funded, so the summary needs to name the source of that $33,000.

2. **Is the June departure being refilled?** If that attorney is replaced from existing funds, the grant really adds a third attorney. If not, the grant would mostly keep you at two. I need to know which so the summary describes it accurately, since a reviewer could easily read it as a replacement.

3. **How many more tenants a year would a third attorney serve?** Your two attorneys handled 163 cases last year, so roughly 80 each. Is that the right figure for a new hire, or would a first-year attorney take fewer? If you have a ballpark, I'll use it to show how much of the ~300 turn-aways you'd cover.

4. **When would the hire start?** For example, a summer 2027 start overlapping with the departing attorney, or later.

5. **What are the foundation's stated priorities or scoring criteria?** For example access to justice, underserved counties, or sustainability after the grant ends. Please also give me the clinic and county names if you want them in the summary.

If you don't know an answer, just say so and I'll write around it without guessing. One note: since you don't have a figure for tenants without a lawyer, I'll present the 58% as your clients' outcomes, not as proof that representation caused them. Reviewers at a bar foundation are likely to catch that distinction.

1. A family fund has pledged $20,000 a year for two years toward the new attorney. The rest of the gap comes from our general budget. The county contract is up for renewal in October, and I can't promise it will be renewed.

2. I don't know.

3. I don't know.

4. No set date. The attorney who's leaving in June has agreed to spend her last month training the new hire. The foundation decides in May. Our last attorney opening took 5 months to fill.

5. I don't know the foundation's scoring criteria. The clinic is the Tenant Defense Project. I don't have the county name to give you.

I've written the summary from your facts and left out anything you didn't know. It's about 250 words.

<final_document>
**Tenant Defense Project: A Third Eviction Defense Attorney**

Last year, 1,140 eviction cases were filed in our county. The Tenant Defense Project represented the tenant in 163 of them. We turned away about 300 more tenants because no attorney was free to take their case.

Our attorneys are at capacity. Each of our two attorneys carries about 80 open cases, and one of them leaves in June.

The tenants we do represent often keep their homes or gain time to move. In 58% of last year's cases, our client either stayed in the home or secured at least 60 days to relocate.

We request $90,000 over two years ($45,000 per year) to hire a third staff attorney, so that fewer tenants are turned away for lack of an available lawyer.

**Funding plan.** The position costs $78,000 per year, including benefits. The grant and a family fund's two-year pledge of $20,000 per year together cover $65,000 per year, or 83% of the cost. The Tenant Defense Project will pay the remaining $13,000 per year from its general budget. Our core operations also rely on a $60,000 annual county contract that comes up for renewal in October. Because outside funds cover most of the new position's cost, it does not depend on that renewal.

**Reporting.** Each year of the grant, we will report how many tenants we represented, how many we turned away, and our case outcomes, measured the same way as the 58% figure above.
</final_document>

**Things to check before you submit:**

- **Training timeline:** I didn't include the plan for the departing attorney to train the new hire. The foundation decides in May, she leaves in June, and your last hire took five months. That training only works if you hire before you know about the award. If you plan to do that, add a sentence saying so, because it would be a strong point.
- **"Third attorney":** If the June vacancy won't be refilled, this grant keeps you at two attorneys instead of adding a third. Reviewers will notice. In that case, retitle it and describe the request as keeping your capacity from dropping.
- **County contract:** I mentioned it openly and made the point that the new position mostly doesn't depend on it. Reviewers asking about sustainability will probably find out about the renewal anyway, so it's better they hear it from you. You can cut it if you'd rather.
- **Reporting:** That paragraph is a commitment I added. Keep it only if you can track turn-aways and outcomes every year.
- **Missing name:** Replace "our county" with the county's name when you have it.
